title: Optimization and kinetic study of chemical‐free froth flotation for waste broken split chickpea protein recovery
content:
Abstract

BACKGROUND

The increasing demand for plant-based proteins has intensified the need for sustainable separation technologies to recover protein-rich fractions from agricultural by-products. This study investigated froth flotation, a chemical-free separation technique, to recover protein from broken split chickpea flour and to produce functional, protein-rich ingredients.

RESULTS

The effects of operating parameters on protein recovery were investigated, and the optimum conditions were identified as a feed mass of 100 g, pH 7, an airflow rate of 8 L min−1, and a flotation time of 20 min. Kinetic analysis indicated that the second-order Arbiter model provided the best fit to the experimental protein recovery data. Under the optimum conditions, the protein concentrate achieved an enrichment ratio of 2.77 and a protein recovery of approximately 42%. Scanning electron microscopy and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy supported the separation of protein-rich and starch-rich fractions, while differential scanning calorimetry indicated that the thermal stability of the protein was retained following flotation. The concentrate exhibited a water-holding capacity of 2.67 g g−1, an oil-holding capacity of 2.18 g g−1, a foaming capacity of 3.23 mL, a bulk density of 0.422 g mL−1, and a tapped density of 0.53 g mL−1.

CONCLUSION

Froth flotation demonstrated potential as a simple separation technique for recovering protein-rich fractions from broken split chickpea flour. The combination of protein enrichment, moderate recovery, and retained thermal stability suggests that the process could support the valorization of chickpea processing by-products into functional food ingredients. Further studies on process optimization, scalability, and resource consumption are required to establish its industrial feasibility. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
